title: The Optimal Can
primary_metric: the retooling's net annual material-cost savings expressed as a payback period in months, evaluated against plant leadership's stated capital-approval payback ceiling

options.A: Hold The Line — keep the industry-standard can body, zero retooling cost
options.B: The Slim Retool — re-cut the forming dies to the calculus-optimal proportions

concept_sheet: C3 — The Optimal Can (brainstorm sheet, tier Advanced)

deliverables.text: The surface-area function for a closed cylinder of fixed volume, written symbolically as a function of radius alone, S(r), with the fixed-volume substitution shown, and its derivative dS/dr found using the power rule and reported as the instantaneous rate of change of surface area with respect to radius.

The critical-point work: dS/dr set equal to zero and solved for the critical radius r*, followed by the first derivative test (or an equivalent concavity check) proving r* is a local minimum of S(r) and not a local maximum, with the resulting height h* computed from r* and the fixed volume.

A material-cost comparison table: total surface area, aluminum weight, and material cost per can for Hold The Line's body versus The Slim Retool's body, with the percent reduction in surface area and in cost shown.

An annual-savings and payback calculation at Ridgeline's stated annual can volume for this line: net annual material savings, the retooling cost's payback period in months, and a break-even calculation for the minimum annual can volume at which The Slim Retool pays back within plant leadership's stated capital-approval window.

appendices.title: Production Volume, Retooling Cost, and the Payback Bar

balance.argument_a: At the stated retooling cost ($600,000, MA2) and Ridgeline's stated annual volume (300,000,000 cans/yr, MA3), The Slim Retool saves only $0.000938 per can (2.0866% of Hold The Line's $0.044933 material cost), or $281,268.82/yr. Payback is 25.60 months, about 6.24% longer than plant leadership's stated 24-month ceiling. The shape genuinely uses less metal on every can, forever, and it still does not clear the bar this year.
balance.argument_b: The saving is small per can but permanent: every can stamped on this line for the tooling's working life carries the same 2.09% material-cost reduction. The case's own break-even shows the gap to approval is narrow -- Ridgeline would only need 319,978,587 cans/yr (about 6.7% more than the stated 300,000,000) for the retooling to clear the 24-month ceiling on its own numbers, and a contract canner's volume on any one client line is exactly the kind of figure that moves with a single new contract.
balance.margin_basis: margin_pct = the percentage by which the retooling's actual annual material savings falls short of the annual savings required to hit plant leadership's stated payback ceiling. annual_savings = (S_std - S_opt) x thickness x density x price_per_lb x annual_can_volume = $281,268.82; required_annual_savings = retool_cost / (ceiling_months/12) = $600,000 / 2 = $300,000.00; margin_pct = (required_annual_savings - annual_savings) / required_annual_savings x 100 = 6.24. Hold The Line wins on the case's own numbers, but narrowly, and the verdict is directly sensitive to MA1 (sheet thickness), MA2 (retooling cost) and MA3 (annual volume) -- flexing any single one +/-50% is enough to flip the recommendation in either direction.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Can-body sheet thickness (gauge), held identical for both options
modeling_assumptions.basis: Trade/technical sources describe modern DWI beverage-can sidewalls as roughly 0.0037-0.0049 in thick; no single manufacturer or standards-body datasheet stating an exact gauge was located and fetched to a primary source, so this case fixes the midpoint of that commonly cited range.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Affects only the absolute weight/dollar figures and the payback period (linear multiplier); cannot change the thickness-independent surface-area percent comparison. At -50% (0.00215 in) payback stretches to ~51 months; at +50% (0.00645 in) payback drops to ~17 months -- alone enough to flip the verdict in either direction against the 24-month ceiling.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Retooling cost: die-and-tooling changeover on Ridgeline's existing Line 3 equipment to the new body diameter
modeling_assumptions.basis: No public price exists for this specific one-off changeover. The case fixes a value representative of a die-and-tooling-only changeover (new die sets, neck/flange re-tooling, changeover trials) rather than a full new production line.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Linearly load-bearing on payback. At -50% ($300,000) payback drops to ~13 months (clears the 24-month ceiling); at +50% ($900,000) payback stretches to ~38 months (misses by a wide margin).

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Ridgeline Canning's annual can production volume on this line
modeling_assumptions.basis: Ridgeline is fictional, so no public production figure exists. Grounded in real published can-line throughput (modern high-speed lines run roughly 2,000-2,400 cans/minute at full rate); 300 million cans/yr on one contract-canner line running well under full-rate, round-the-clock operation is an ordinary volume for a mid-size line.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: Linearly load-bearing on payback, opposite direction from MA2. At -50% (150M cans/yr) payback stretches to ~51 months; at +50% (450M cans/yr) payback drops to ~17 months.

modeling_assumptions.assumption: Plant leadership's capital-approval payback ceiling for a line-level retooling request
modeling_assumptions.basis: Ridgeline's specific finance policy is not public. A payback period of roughly one to three years is widely described in general capital-budgeting practice as an acceptable range for manufacturing equipment investments; this case fixes Ridgeline's policy at the middle of that range.
modeling_assumptions.sensitivity: This is the threshold, not an input to the payback calculation -- it does not change the computed 25.60-month payback, only whether that period counts as a 'yes.' Moving it to 30 months flips the verdict to B at the base-case figures; moving it to 20 months widens A's margin.

sensitivity_disclosure.justification: MA1: no manufacturer or standards-body datasheet states an exact beverage-can sidewall gauge; the case fixes the midpoint of the sourced trade-literature thickness range as a documented estimate, not a vendor spec, so the exact figure is inherently a proprietary-adjacent estimate rather than a citable fact.

MA2: die-and-tooling changeover pricing for a specific line's diameter conversion is not publicly quoted anywhere; the case fixes a representative changeover-scale figure as a documented estimate rather than a real vendor quote, which is the proprietary-inaccessible exception, not a sourced fact.

MA3: Ridgeline Canning is a fictional company, so no real production-volume record for this line can exist to cite; the figure is grounded in published real-world can-line throughput rates as the closest public analogue, which is a one-time estimate, not a citable production record.

MA4: Ridgeline's internal capital-approval payback policy is a fictional company's stated policy with no public record to cite; the case fixes it at the middle of the generally cited manufacturing capital-budgeting payback range as a documented estimate, not a sourced company figure.

overview_numerals_cleared.why: 'Line 3' -- the production line's label in the plant, texture only. Never used in any calculation; the case's own model numbers (radius, volume, cost) are all introduced later in the Background and Appendices, not the Overview.

reinforcement_note: Checked all 25 skills with n=0 in Calculus at authoring time (limits/continuity, chain/product/quotient rule, integrals, applications of integrals, series). This case's real math -- substituting V=pi*r^2*h into surface area S(r)=2*pi*r^2+2V/r and differentiating via the power rule to find the critical radius -- is the same technique Curves Turn already claims (power rule, critical point, first-derivative test, local min/max, concavity). No chain/product/quotient rule, limit, integral, or series step appears anywhere in D1-D4's actual derivation. Publishing as a reinforcement case: same skill, a genuinely different real-world story and career (packaging/process engineering) for variety.
